A Little-Known Fuel Deficit That Makes Women Over 45 Feel Like They're Losing Their Mind

If you lose words mid-sentence, forget why you walked into a room, and your doctor keeps saying "everything looks normal," read this short article before you try another supplement or another round of bloodwork.

14,283 Ratings
Women's Health · Perimenopause · Brain Science
By Dr. Catherine Langford, Neuroendocrinologist | March 26, 2026

I'm Dr. Catherine Langford, a neuroendocrinologist based in Philadelphia.

Over 18 years studying why brains fail, I've worked with more than 1,000 women who sat across from me, eyes wet, and said the same sentence: "I feel like I'm losing my mind." Most of them were experiencing some version of the same invisible problem...

  • Losing words mid-sentence
  • Reading the same paragraph three times
  • Freezing at green lights and in meetings
  • Googling "dementia" at 2am in secret

Whatever the version,

I've seen it.

From the fog that never lifts... To the fake nods in every meeting...


The Word That Vanished At The Podium In Front Of 200 Colleagues

It wasn't until earlier this year that I finally found the key to what was actually happening inside the brain of every woman I'd been failing to help.

It began with a moment at a neurology conference that left me speechless. Literally.

One evening, pulling my own research back off the shelf, I stumbled on a line I'd written six years earlier — and had never once applied to myself. The line changed everything.

The Surprising Truth: Your Brain Ran Out Of Fuel

Everyone talks about hormones.

Every woman over 45 has heard about estrogen, progesterone, HRT.

But almost nobody is talking about what hormone loss does to your brain's fuel supply.

Here's what your brain is actually doing all day:

The drawing above shows a fully-fueled brain on the left compared to a fuel-depleted brain on the right.

To understand the difference between them, we need to start with How Your Brain Actually Gets Its Energy.

Something was running the engine — and something was running out.

She had seen this pattern for years. Fully-fueled brains keep thoughts arriving on time. Depleted brains hesitate mid-sentence, then hesitate again, then hesitate for good.

That's what a fully-fueled brain looks like.

Now take a look at the following picture.

The first noticeable difference is the dim, slow-firing activity at the top, right?

Well, this happens because the creatine that usually recharges ATP is no longer arriving in the amounts your brain needs, leading to slower thinking and eventually the feeling of fog.

It's similar to driving a car that's running on fumes.

The engine still turns over, but it can't climb a hill. Every thought takes more effort than it used to.

If We Don't Refuel The Brain Directly, The Fog Will Keep Getting Thicker

When this occurs, the demands of a working day start outrunning your brain's energy supply, resulting in the fog creeping into every part of your life.

And like a tank running dry... the thoughts have nowhere to come from... So your mind begins to stall.

Feeling slow, foggy and distant.

All of a sudden, every meeting feels like your thoughts are moving through cotton wool, making it impossible for you to trust yourself.

Even the simplest conversations become unbearable.

Did You Know That Women Carry Less Creatine Than Men Across The Entire Lifespan?

Consider this... whenever estrogen begins to drop in perimenopause, the fuel system starts changing too...

Emerging research shows creatine metabolism may be disrupted further as hormones shift, leaving the brain even more exposed.

This disruption quietly starves the brain of the compound it needs most, exactly when you need it most.

This is really important...

Because unlike blood sugar... the brain doesn't have a reserve tank. When creatine runs low, thinking runs slow.

This Isn't Who You're Becoming. It's What Your Brain Is Running Out Of.

It wasn't declining. It was depleting.

Dr. Langford was rereading a cellular metabolism file the lab had kept for brain-energy research. One line stopped her. She had co-authored it six years earlier and never once applied it to the fog that had been walking into her office for a decade. The human brain is 2% of body weight and burns 20% of the body's total energy. That energy runs on ATP. And ATP, inside a firing neuron, is recharged by one specific compound. Creatine.

Women's bodies carry significantly lower creatine stores than men's to begin with. When estrogen drops in perimenopause, the pathway that keeps creatine replenished slows. The brain, which already ran on tighter margins, now runs on fumes.

The research had been sitting in journals for twenty years. Meta-analyses showing creatine sharpens working memory, processing speed, and word retrieval. A peer-reviewed trial measured a 16.4% increase in frontal brain creatine after eight weeks of daily supplementation in perimenopausal women. Nobody had connected the dots for this audience. The hormone researchers weren't reading the metabolism papers. The metabolism researchers weren't reading the hormone papers.

She had a name for it within the hour. The Brain Fuel Deficit.

And unlike decline, a fuel deficit is refillable.

The Lecture Where She Didn't Lose A Single Word

She started taking pharmaceutical-grade creatine monohydrate herself. The exact dose the research had tested. Every morning. No protocol yet. Just the compound and her own brain.

Week one, nothing dramatic. The research had told her to expect that. Saturation takes time.

Week two, something subtle shifted. She caught herself mid-lecture and the word was just there. Waiting. No scramble, no filler, no let me rephrase. It had arrived on time.

Somewhere between Day 14 and Day 30, right in the window the research predicted, the cotton-wool feeling lifted. Not reduced. Gone. She sat at her desk at 4pm and realized she had worked three straight hours without that familiar feeling of her brain slowly powering down.

By Day 30, she felt like herself again. The version she thought she had lost somewhere in her mid-forties and was never getting back. She trusted her own brain for the first time in years.

That is when she decided to stop handing her patients a shelf-pointing recommendation toward the vitamin aisle and start building something engineered for exactly this audience, exactly this dose, exactly this compliance problem.

It works completely differently to menopause blends, antidepressants, brain games and expensive 15-ingredient multi-formulas.

Ember fully leverages the clinical research on creatine monohydrate to target one specific mechanism: the Brain Fuel Deficit that opens when estrogen drops and creatine goes with it.

This "gummy" isn't a novelty or a marketing trick.

This allows the protocol to become a habit instead of another bottle pushed to the back of the cabinet...

And it's this consistent, daily intake that helps refill the brain's fuel reserves and restore the thoughts, words, and confidence perimenopause has been draining.

I can think in full sentences again.
